strengths: Novel latent-space formulation for privacy preservation that is practical for large video foundation models, avoiding expensive retraining required by pixel-level methods

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five diverse downstream tasks (action recognition on 3 datasets, temporal action detection, anomaly detection) demonstrating strong generalization to unseen tasks
Lightweight and scalable solution with 88.7% fewer trainable parameters than prior work, enabling easy application to frozen encoders and large pretrained models
Well-designed training framework with three complementary objectives, validated through extensive ablation studies showing necessity of each component
Impressive data efficiency: effective generalization from small datasets like HMDB51 with minimal performance degradation on unseen tasks
First systematic evaluation and mitigation of gender bias in video action recognition models, showing 39-42% bias reduction
Clear presentation with strong motivation, well-structured methodology, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited formal privacy analysis: no differential privacy bounds or theoretical privacy guarantees; relies on single metric (cMAP on VISPR); no quantitative verification that mutual information is minimized; threat model limited to linear classifiers

Insufficient justification for core technical choices: NT-Xent loss as privacy objective lacks rigorous justification beyond intuition; simple L2 consistency loss (Eq. 6) not ablated against alternatives; connection between contrastive similarity and information destruction not formally established
Hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly explored: multiple critical parameters (ωLC, ωT, ωB) with ablations only for ωLC; no principled guidance for selecting hyperparameters for new applications

Gender bias evaluation limitations: binary gender formulation acknowledged as non-inclusive but not addressed; limited to gender bias without evaluating other demographics (age, race); artificial bias injection (95-5%) may not reflect realistic distributions; unclear whether improvements stem from privacy or feature distortion

Temporal attribute vulnerability: Table 6 reveals dramatic performance gaps without latent consistency (26.67% vs 69.73%), indicating complementary failure modes and suggesting method may not robustly protect all sensitive information

Limited baseline comparisons: main comparisons against SPAct and TeD-SPAD from same research group; no comparison with orthogonal privacy approaches (federated learning, differential privacy, secure computation)
Reproducibility concerns: project page URL not provided; code availability not explicitly mentioned; some implementation details potentially unclear for reproduction

Privacy evaluation limited to linear classifiers on a small set of attributes; no analysis of information theoretically what remains in anonymized features; no evaluation against non-linear privacy attacks

strengths: Practical problem formulation addressing real limitations of pixel-level anonymization (computational efficiency, multi-task applicability)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets, backbones, and baselines with extensive ablations
Strong empirical results demonstrating 35% privacy improvement while maintaining utility within 1-2% across diverse downstream tasks
Multi-task generalization without task-specific retraining, a clear advantage over prior work (SPAct, TeD-SPAD)
Data efficiency and practical applicability—88.7% fewer trainable parameters than baseline methods
Novel contribution to fairness through gender bias evaluation protocols and demonstration that privacy preservation aids fairness
Clear presentation with good motivation and well-structured evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (transformer encoder, SimCLR NT-Xent loss, L2 regularization) are well-established; contribution is primarily formulation rather than methodological innovation
Inadequate privacy evaluation—only weak threat model (linear classifier); no evaluation against stronger attacks (membership inference, model inversion, deeper classifiers, adversarial attacks)
No formal privacy guarantees or information-theoretic analysis; unvalidated claim that NT-Xent loss on random frame pairs minimizes mutual information

Fundamental tension between privacy objective (remove information) and latent consistency objective (preserve features close to original); Table 5 shows complete failure without LLC, suggesting core approach is fragile rather than principled
Overstated generalization claims: method is trained on AR+TAD+AD then evaluated on same tasks; Table 4 shows non-trivial performance drops on unseen tasks

Gender bias evaluation limited to binary gender (acknowledged as non-inclusive), artificial bias creation, and only one real-world dataset; unclear whether improvements come from removing gender-specific information vs. degrading all tasks equally
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or error bars; no code release mentioned; reproducibility concerns
Missing mechanistic explanation of how clip-level AAM destroys spatial information while preserving temporal; insufficient justification for why self-attention specifically helps (Table 8)
Incomplete privacy analysis: paper doesn't analyze per-attribute privacy (VISPR has 7 attributes) or robustness to adversarial attacks; temporal attributes inadequately protected (Table 6)
Limited scope: only RGB video, assumes frozen encoders, dismisses transmission threat model without adequate mitigation strategy

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: novel shift from pixel-level to latent-space anonymization with clear practical advantages for frozen foundation models

Unprecedented multi-task generalization: first method to preserve privacy across five diverse downstream tasks (3 action recognition datasets, temporal action detection, anomaly detection) with minimal performance loss (<2%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: extensive ablations (Tables 3-6, 8-10), evaluation across 5 video backbones, and novel gender bias evaluation protocols with real-world validation

Technically sound design: clip-level self-supervised privacy objective (Eq. 5) and latent consistency loss (Eq. 6) are well-motivated; three-way loss optimization (Eq. 7) elegantly balances competing objectives
Strong practical efficiency: 88.7% fewer trainable parameters, ~3.5× faster training than baselines, scales to billion-parameter foundation models
Unique gender bias contribution: introduces first protocols for assessing and mitigating gender bias in action recognition, achieving 42.3% and 39.5% relative reductions in subclass gaps
Demonstrates data efficiency: method generalizes across tasks when trained on small datasets like HMDB51 (Table 3)
weaknesses: Limited component-level novelty: NT-Xent loss (SimCLR), L2 regularization, and self-attention adapters are standard techniques; novelty lies primarily in problem formulation and application rather than algorithmic innovation

Inadequate privacy evaluation: (1) only evaluates 7 VISPR attributes and gait; (2) uses weak threat model (linear classifier) without adversarial classifiers, membership inference, or model inversion attacks; (3) lacks formal privacy guarantees or differential privacy analysis; (4) unclear if 35% privacy reduction generalizes to other attributes/attacks

Gender bias evaluation limitations: (1) binary gender formulation acknowledged as non-inclusive; (2) only addresses gender, ignoring race, age, ethnicity; (3) artificial 95%-5% bias injection may not reflect real patterns; (4) single real-world dataset (elderly subjects only)
Hyperparameter selection appears empirically driven: ωLC=100, ωT=1, ωB=1 lack clear justification; Table 9 shows sensitivity but no principled selection procedure provided

Privacy-utility tradeoff analysis limited to one dataset: Figure 3 only shows PA-HMDB51; multi-dataset curves would strengthen claims; only compares against pixel-level methods, missing broader privacy literature

Temporal attribute defense ambiguity: Table 6 reveals that latent consistency preserves some temporal structure useful for gait recognition (53.45% vs 26.67% without LC), making the claim about defending temporal attributes conditional and potentially contradicting utility preservation
Generalization concerns: all experiments use Kinetics400 pretraining; unknown how method transfers to models pretrained on different distributions or substantially different video domains

Missing implementation details: project page blank, code availability not mentioned, static clip sampling procedure not formally specified, batch size sensitivity not analyzed despite appearing in Eq. 5

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: latent-space anonymization for video foundation models addresses a timely challenge with clear real-world applicability and advantages over pixel-level methods

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: extensive experiments across 5+ downstream tasks, multiple datasets (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51, THUMOS14, UCF-Crime), and different architectures (I3D, VideoMAE, VJEPA, InternVideo), with thorough ablations
Strong empirical results: achieves 35% reduction in privacy leakage while maintaining near-baseline utility (within 1-2%), demonstrating effective privacy-utility tradeoff across diverse tasks

Practical and efficient design: lightweight AAM with 88.7% fewer parameters than prior methods, no retraining required, 3.5x faster training, works across frozen models and scales to large foundation models

Well-designed training framework: three complementary objectives (clip-level self-supervised privacy, co-training utility, latent consistency) with latent consistency loss being particularly clever for preventing overfitting to proxy tasks

Novel contribution on fairness: first work to introduce evaluation protocols for gender bias in video action recognition, demonstrating that privacy preservation also mitigates gender bias (39.5-42.3% gap reduction)
Robustness analysis: evaluates black-box and white-box attacks, reconstruction attacks, temporal attributes (gait), and generalizes to unseen tasks with data efficiency on small datasets
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty: adapts NT-Xent loss from prior work (Dave et al. 2022b, Fioresi et al. 2023) to latent space; main contribution is L2 consistency regularizer, which while effective, represents incremental technical advance

Informal privacy model: lacks formal privacy definitions (e.g., differential privacy, information-theoretic bounds), evaluates only against supervised attribute classifiers, assumes adversary has both features and labels, making threat model limited and unclear

White-box vulnerability: privacy cMAP of 73.7% under white-box attacks vs. 58.8% under black-box (Table 8) represents significant gap; limited discussion of defenses or mitigation strategies for high-security scenarios

Weak theoretical justification: lacks rigorous explanation for why minimizing static-clip mutual information removes privacy-sensitive attributes like gender; missing analysis of what spatial vs. temporal information is preserved/removed

Restricted applicability: only works for global-embedding tasks, cannot handle dense predictions (segmentation, captioning); binary gender formulation limits fairness claims despite acknowledgment; scope narrower than claimed in abstract

Hyperparameter sensitivity: multiple hyperparameters (ωLC=100, ωT, ωB) with non-monotonic sensitivity; limited guidance for practitioners; Table 4 suggests task-specific tuning needed despite claims of generalizability

Limited unseen task evaluation: only 3 proxy tasks in training; 'unseen' tasks mostly evaluated via Table 5 ablation; single-architecture evaluation for truly new tasks (retrieval, Table 13); no evaluation on other common video tasks

Incomplete statistical rigor: no error bars, standard deviations, or significance testing reported; unclear if results are single runs or averaged; reproducibility details regarding seeds and multiple runs missing

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing practical latent-space privacy for video foundation models
Comprehensive multi-task evaluation across 5 distinct downstream tasks, significantly more thorough than prior pixel-level work
Computationally efficient plug-and-play adapter (88.7% fewer parameters, works across different backbones, ~3.5x faster than baselines)
Extensive ablation studies covering architecture choices, loss components, hyperparameter sensitivity, and dataset scaling
Novel contribution of formalized gender bias evaluation protocols (NTU-Bias, Toyota Smarthome) for action recognition
Strong empirical results: ~35% privacy leakage reduction with 1-2% utility maintenance across tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (NT-Xent privacy loss, L2 latent consistency, task-specific losses) are straightforward applications of existing techniques without methodological innovation
Vulnerable privacy evaluation: Non-robust to white-box attacks (Table 8), empirical privacy via classifier performance rather than formal guarantees, threat model not formalized
Overstated generalization claims: Method trains on 3 tasks (AR, TAD, AD) with non-negligible drops on unseen tasks (Table 5: ~1-2% drops), true cross-task generalization not demonstrated
Weak latent consistency loss justification: Why L2 distance? Fundamental tension between preserving latent structure and removing private information not addressed
Gender bias evaluation limitations: Binary gender labels (acknowledged as 'not ideal'), artificial spurious correlations in NTU-Bias protocol, mechanism linking privacy to bias mitigation unexplored

Hyperparameter sensitivity and reproducibility concerns: ωLC varies dramatically (Table 11), no statistical significance testing, random seeds not mentioned, optimal hyperparameter selection not justified
Incomplete threat model: Only static visual attributes evaluated, no membership inference or sophisticated attacks considered, white-box vulnerability dismissed as 'unrealistic'
Dense task applicability limited: Method only handles global-embedding tasks (acknowledged limitation), cannot extend to segmentation or frame-level predictions
Technical clarity issues: Static clip sampling procedure undefined, variable-length video handling unspecified, temporal attribute privacy (Table 7) explanation vague

Missing comparisons: No comparison with other latent-space privacy methods, differential privacy approaches, or federated learning privacy techniques; limited justification for latent-space superiority

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: First latent-space anonymization method that enables multi-task privacy preservation without retraining foundation models, directly addressing practical limitations of existing pixel-level approaches

Comprehensive technical design: Three synergistic training objectives (self-supervised privacy, co-training utility, latent consistency) are well-justified; temporal clip-level anonymization is a thoughtful design choice

Rigorous and extensive evaluation: Evaluates on 5 downstream tasks, multiple video encoders (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), comprehensive privacy protocols (VISPR, VP-HMDB51/UCF101, Casia-B gait), novel bias evaluation protocols, and attack resistance analysis

Strong empirical results: 35% privacy leakage reduction with only 1-2% utility degradation; first to generalize across diverse tasks without task-specific fine-tuning; data-efficient; scales to large foundation models; reduces gender bias by 39.5-42.3%

Exceptional practical efficiency: 88.7% fewer trainable parameters, ~3.5x faster training, plug-and-play applicability to frozen encoders, enables feature precomputation (4 min + 1.4 min training vs 185 min baseline)

Comprehensive reproducibility: Detailed implementation specs (Appendix B), complete training algorithm (Appendix D), extensive ablations (Tables 5-7, 10-12) supporting design choices, clear hyperparameter specifications
Well-written presentation: Clear motivation, effective figures (especially Figure 2 workflow), honest limitation discussion, well-organized appendices
weaknesses: Limited privacy guarantees and threat model: No formal differential privacy or information-theoretic bounds; privacy evaluated indirectly via downstream classifiers; not robust to white-box attacks (cMAP 73.7 vs baseline 76.4 when attacker has full access); connection between mutual information minimization and overall privacy removal not rigorously established

Scope limitations restrict applicability: Cannot protect patch-wise embeddings (dense prediction tasks), cannot protect pre-transmission scenarios, only handles global clip-level embeddings; these substantially narrow deployment scenarios despite being acknowledged

Temporal privacy attribute vulnerability: Table 7 shows concerning results—without latent consistency, gait recognition (temporal attribute) cMAP drops to 26.67, but WITH it only 53.45; suggests inadequate temporal privacy protection when generalization is prioritized; proposed solution (adding temporal task to privacy loss) is ad-hoc and not evaluated in main results

Binary gender formulation undermines fairness claims: Authors acknowledge formulation is 'not ideal and not inclusive' but don't address this limitation; no evaluation on other protected attributes (age, skin color, disability); fairness contribution generalizability questionable

Latent consistency loss may limit privacy: Forcing features close to original space could fundamentally limit privacy gains; trade-off between privacy and generalization not thoroughly analyzed; choice of L2 distance regularizer not justified against alternatives

Hyperparameter sensitivity underexplored: Multiple hyperparameters (ωLC=100, ωT=1, ωB=1) lack comprehensive sensitivity analysis; while Table 11 ablates ωLC, sensitivity to ωT and ωB unexplored; guidance for setting parameters on new domains/tasks missing

Limited baseline comparisons and privacy-utility tradeoff analysis: Comparisons primarily against SPAct (2022) and TeD-SPAD (2023); only one tradeoff curve (Figure 3, single dataset); how tradeoff changes across tasks/datasets unclear; limited guidance for practitioners selecting privacy-utility balance

Privacy evaluation limitations: VISPR is primarily image-based; VP-HMDB51/UCF101 are small-scale; evaluation on larger, more diverse video privacy datasets needed; reconstruction attacks only tested on limited datasets; missing analysis of clip sampling strategy sensitivity and architectural failure modes
